title: Why the Orthodox Church rejects the Papacy
subtitle: There is no first throne above the Church; the Council is the seat of authority.
summary: Universal jurisdiction, papal infallibility, and the development of supremacy at Rome are rejected on conciliar and patristic grounds. The fiercest witnesses are Pope Gregory the Great himself, Cyprian of Carthage, Firmilian of Caesarea, John Chrysostom, Theodoret of Cyrus, the Synod of Douzy, and the wider conciliar settlement at Chalcedon and Constantinople IV.
origin: Discord, dogma-exegesis: Why does the Orthodox Church reject Papacy?

essay.text: The Orthodox Church does not reject the Petrine office. She honours Peter as the prince of the apostles. What she rejects is the later doctrine that one bishop, the Bishop of Rome, holds universal jurisdiction over the Church and, since 1870, possesses an infallible teaching authority that does not derive from a council. The two are different claims. The first is patristic; the second is a medieval and modern development that the Fathers, including the Popes of Rome themselves up to the seventh century, explicitly refuse.
Gregory the Great refuses to be called Universal Bishop

When the Patriarch of Constantinople allowed himself to be addressed as Ecumenical (Universal) Patriarch, Pope Gregory the Great wrote to the Emperor Maurice and to his brother bishops in fury. The title "Universal Bishop," he says, was first offered by the Council of Chalcedon to the See of Rome, and "no one of my predecessors has ever consented to use this so profane a title." Anyone who covets it "is in his elation the precursor of Antichrist." Gregory does not soften this: the bishop who exalts himself over all others, in his very title, prefigures the man of lawlessness. The Roman See itself, in the seventh century, refuses the substance of what later Rome will claim.
The chair of Peter is in three Sees, not one

Gregory writes to Eulogius of Alexandria that the See of Peter is not Rome alone, but Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch, where Peter founded, taught, and sat. "Since then it is the See of one, and one See, over which by divine authority three bishops now preside, whatever good I hear of you, this I impute to myself." Chrysostom says of his own bishop Flavian of Antioch: "though we do not retain the body of Peter, we do retain the faith of Peter, and retaining the faith of Peter we have Peter." The Petrine principle is the apostolic faith, held by the body of bishops, not the geographical possession of a single chair.
Cyprian: the Church is established in the bishops, plural

Cyprian of Carthage states the conciliar principle plainly: "the Church is founded upon the bishops, and every act of the Church is controlled by these same rulers." The keys are given to Peter to manifest the unity of the apostolic college, but "the rest of the apostles were also the same as was Peter, endowed with a like partnership both of honour and power." When Pope Stephen of Rome attempted to enforce his ruling on the rebaptism of heretics on the African Church, his peer Firmilian of Caesarea answered him directly: "I am justly indignant at this so open and manifest folly of Pope Stephen, that he who so boasts of the place of his episcopate, and contends that he holds the succession from Peter, should introduce many other rocks and establish new buildings of many churches." A third-century bishop, addressing a third-century Pope as a peer, by name.
The conciliar canons against universal jurisdiction

Canon 6 of the First Ecumenical Council (Nicaea, 325) regulates the jurisdiction of Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch within their own territorial provinces and explicitly recognises ancient customs of equal patriarchal jurisdiction. Canon 28 of Chalcedon (451) grants to the See of Constantinople equal privileges with the See of Old Rome, on the ground that both Sees received their primacy because of the imperial standing of their cities. Pope Leo refused this canon; the Council passed it without him. The Synod of Douzy (871) writes to Pope Hadrian II refusing to surrender to Rome the right of a local synod to try its own bishops, citing Nicaea: "individual metropolitans ought to have jurisdiction over a single province, and no two provinces should be under the rule of one." The conciliar mind, repeatedly, is jurisdiction by province and patriarchate, never universal.
Popes who fell, popes who failed

If the See of Rome were infallible by office, no occupant could fall. The historical record refuses the claim. Liberius signed an Arian-leaning creed under pressure; Jerome records it. Honorius I was condemned by name as a heretic by the Sixth Ecumenical Council (Constantinople III, 681), and the condemnation was repeated by his successors. Vigilius wavered on the condemnation of the Three Chapters until the Council of Constantinople II forced his hand. Each is a stone removed from the foundation of papal infallibility.

florilegium.author: Pope St Gregory the Great
florilegium.text: I confidently say that whosoever calls himself, or desires to be called, Universal Priest, is in his elation the precursor of Antichrist, because he proudly puts himself above all others. For, as that perverse one wishes to appear as above all men, so whosoever this one is who covets being called sole priest, he extols himself above all other priests.
florilegium.gloss: A reigning Bishop of Rome, in the seventh century, calls the title that later Rome will claim the title of the precursor of Antichrist.

florilegium.author: Pope St Gregory the Great
florilegium.text: This name of Universality was offered by the holy synod of Chalcedon to the pontiff of the Apostolic See which by the providence of God I serve. But no one of my predecessors has ever consented to use this so profane a title; since, if one patriarch is called Universal, the name of patriarch in the case of the rest is derogated. But far be this from the mind of a Christian, that any one should wish to seize for himself that whereby he might seem in the least degree to lessen the honour of his brethren.
florilegium.gloss: Gregory expressly denies that any of his predecessors ever accepted the title of universal bishop, even when it was offered by an Ecumenical Council.

florilegium.author: Pope St Gregory the Great
florilegium.text: Your most sweet Holiness has spoken much in your letter to me about the chair of St Peter, Prince of the apostles, saying that he himself now sits on it in the persons of his successors. He himself exalted the See in which he deigned even to rest and end the present life (Rome). He himself adorned the See to which he sent his disciple as evangelist (Alexandria). He himself established the See in which, though he was to leave it, he sat for seven years (Antioch). Since then it is the See of one, and one See, over which by divine authority three bishops now preside.
florilegium.gloss: Gregory locates the chair of Peter in three Sees, not in Rome alone; the Patriarch of Alexandria is, in this sense, also a successor of Peter.

florilegium.author: St Cyprian of Carthage
florilegium.work: Treatise 1, On the Unity of the Church
florilegium.text: And although to all the apostles, after his resurrection, he gives an equal power, and says, "As the Father has sent me, even so send I you: Receive the Holy Ghost: whose soever sins you remit, they shall be remitted unto him, and whose soever sins you retain, they shall be retained"; yet, that he might set forth unity, he arranged by his authority the origin of that unity, as beginning from one. Assuredly the rest of the apostles were also the same as was Peter, endowed with a like partnership both of honour and power; but the beginning proceeds from unity.
florilegium.gloss: Peter is the type of unity, not the holder of a jurisdiction above the apostolic college. "The rest of the apostles were also the same as was Peter."

florilegium.author: St Cyprian of Carthage
florilegium.text: Through the changes of times and successions, the ordering of bishops and the plan of the Church flow onwards, so that the Church is founded upon the bishops, and every act of the Church is controlled by these same rulers.
florilegium.gloss: The Church is founded upon the bishops (plural), each in his own See. The act of the Church is the act of the bishops, not of a single bishop ruling over them.

florilegium.author: St Firmilian of Caesarea
florilegium.work: Epistle 75 (preserved in Cyprian, Epistle 74), to Cyprian
florilegium.text: I am justly indignant at this so open and manifest folly of Pope Stephen, that he who so boasts of the place of his episcopate, and contends that he holds the succession from Peter, on whom the foundations of the Church were laid, should introduce many other rocks and establish new buildings of many churches. He does not understand that the truth of the Christian Rock is overshadowed, and in some measure abolished, by him when he thus betrays and deserts unity.
florilegium.gloss: A third-century bishop of Cappadocia rebukes a third-century Pope of Rome by name and openly. Universal jurisdiction is not the operative premise.

florilegium.author: St John Chrysostom
florilegium.text: In speaking of St Peter, the recollection of another Peter has come to me, the common father and teacher (Flavian of Antioch), who has inherited his prowess, and also obtained his chair. For this is the one great privilege of our city, Antioch, that it received the leader of the apostles as its teacher in the beginning. But though we received him as teacher, we did not retain him to the end, but gave him up to royal Rome. Or rather we did retain him to the end, for though we do not retain the body of Peter, we do retain the faith of Peter, and retaining the faith of Peter we have Peter.
florilegium.gloss: Chrysostom: the See of Peter is wherever the faith of Peter is held. Antioch, not Rome alone.

florilegium.author: St John Chrysostom
florilegium.work: Homilies on the Gospel of St Matthew
florilegium.text: Will you that I tell you a fourth proof also of these things? "Peter, do you love me?" says he, "Feed my sheep"; and having asked him a third time, declared this to be an infallible proof of love. But not to priests only is this said, but to every one of us also, who are also entrusted with a little flock.
florilegium.gloss: Chrysostom reads John 21 as binding on every shepherd in the Church, not as a transfer of universal jurisdiction to Peter alone.

florilegium.author: St Jerome of Stridon
florilegium.text: The Church is founded upon Peter, although in another place, the same thing is done upon all the apostles, and they all receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and the strength of the Church is established equally upon them all.
florilegium.gloss: Jerome, the Vulgate translator and the Latin doctor par excellence: the strength of the Church is established equally on all the apostles.

florilegium.author: St Jerome of Stridon
florilegium.text: Pope Liberius, conquered by the tedium of exile and subscribing to heretical wickedness, entered Rome in triumph.
florilegium.gloss: Jerome flatly records that a Pope of Rome signed a heretical formula under pressure. The premise of papal infallibility cannot stand on this historical record.

florilegium.author: Blessed Theodoret of Cyrus
florilegium.text: Dioscorus refuses to abide by these decisions; he is turning the see of the blessed Mark (Alexandria) upside down; and these things he does though he perfectly well knows that the Antiochene metropolis possesses the throne of the great Peter, who was teacher of the blessed Mark, and first and coryphæus of the chorus of the apostles.
florilegium.gloss: Theodoret takes for granted that the Antiochene See possesses the throne of Peter. Peter's chair is not a Roman monopoly.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.text: I shall never be able to persuade myself on these grounds to ignore Meletius, or to forget the Church which is under him, or to treat as small, and of little importance to the true religion, the questions which originated the division. I shall never consent to give in, merely because somebody is very much elated at receiving a letter from men. Even if it had come down from heaven itself, but the bishop does not agree with the sound doctrine of the faith, I cannot look upon him as in communion with the saints.
florilegium.gloss: Basil will not change his judgement on the schism at Antioch on the strength of a Roman letter alone, however much it elevates its recipient. Communion with the saints depends on the sound doctrine of the faith, not on a Roman ratification.

florilegium.author: The Synod of Douzy
florilegium.work: Synodal Letter to Pope Hadrian II
florilegium.text: We fervently beseech your authority to free us from the government of Bishop Hincmar of Laon, as from a great and incorrigible pest. And if, for the time being, it does not please you to put your seal on what we have already lawfully decided in this Synod, may he at least not be restored to his see until he first be re-tried in this province, as the rules and laws require. For until today, no decree of the Fathers has ever denied this privilege to the Churches of France and Belgium; considering especially that the decrees of Nicaea have committed the lesser clergy and even bishops to the authority of their Metropolitans. And as St Boniface explains: "It is proper for us to be diligent guardians of the paternal rules. For no one is ignorant of the constitution of the Nicene Council which decreed that individual metropolitans ought to have jurisdiction over a single province, and that no two provinces should be under the rule of one."
florilegium.gloss: A Frankish synod in 871 tells the Pope of Rome that even with his goodwill it cannot surrender the right of local trial of bishops to a Roman court, and cites Nicaea against him.

florilegium.author: The Synod of Douzy
florilegium.work: Synodal Letter to Pope Hadrian II
florilegium.text: If, far be it, by some suggestion or request, Hincmar wrest a decision from the Apostolic See to be restored to his rank as one scorning and treading upon the holy canons, we will hereafter not recognise any of his decisions, just as until now we have not communed with his deeds by resisting them. For our own holy fathers, who still live with us through their canons, being distinguished in the way of the holy Scriptures and the tradition of the apostles and inspired by the grace of the Holy Spirit, give certain judgement about these things.
florilegium.gloss: A Western synod, openly, in the ninth century: if Rome rules against the canons we will not recognise the decision.

councils.name: First Ecumenical Council, Nicaea
councils.text: Let the ancient customs in Egypt, Libya and Pentapolis prevail, that the Bishop of Alexandria have jurisdiction in all these, since the like is customary for the Bishop of Rome also. Likewise in Antioch and the other provinces, let the Churches retain their privileges. And this is to be universally understood, that if any one be made bishop without the consent of the Metropolitan, the great Synod has declared that such a man ought not to be a bishop.
councils.gloss: Nicaea recognises three patriarchates by analogous jurisdiction, each over its own province. Rome is named alongside Alexandria and Antioch, not above them.

councils.name: Fourth Ecumenical Council, Chalcedon
councils.text: Following in all things the decisions of the holy Fathers, and acknowledging the canon, which has been just read, of the One Hundred and Fifty Bishops beloved-of-God, we also do enact and decree the same things concerning the privileges of the most holy Church of Constantinople, which is New Rome. For the Fathers rightly granted privileges to the throne of old Rome, because it was the royal city. And the One Hundred and Fifty most religious Bishops, actuated by the same consideration, gave equal privileges to the most holy throne of New Rome, justly judging that the city which is honoured with the Sovereignty and the Senate, and enjoys equal privileges with the old imperial Rome, should in ecclesiastical matters also be magnified as she is, and rank next after her.
councils.gloss: Chalcedon grounds the privileges of Old Rome in the civil dignity of the imperial city, not in a unique Petrine inheritance, and grants equal privileges to Constantinople. Pope Leo refused this canon; the Council passed it without him.

councils.name: Sixth Ecumenical Council, Constantinople III
councils.text: And with these we define that there shall be expelled from the holy Church of God and anathematised Honorius who was some time Pope of Old Rome, because of what we found written by him to Sergius, that in all respects he followed his view and confirmed his impious doctrines.
councils.gloss: An Ecumenical Council anathematises a Pope of Rome by name as a heretic. His successors confirmed the anathema. Papal infallibility cannot survive this single fact.

councils.name: Eighth Council, Constantinople IV (879-880, under Photios)
councils.text: We embrace and confess all the holy and ecumenical councils. We anathematise also those who would dare to make an addition or omit anything in the holy Symbol of Faith. Whoever, then, shall arrive at such madness as to write a different Symbol, or to alter that of the holy Fathers, let him be anathema.
councils.gloss: The Photian council, accepted by Roman legates, anathematises the very unilateral edit of the Symbol that Rome would later impose. The decision was a conciliar one, made in the absence of any unilateral Roman ratification.

scripture.note: Upon this rock, read by the Fathers of the faith confessed, not the chair occupied.
Feed my sheep, Chrysostom and Cyprian both apply this charge to all bishops, not to Peter's single successor.
Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth, the binding-and-loosing given to the apostolic body.
The Council of Jerusalem, the conciliar pattern of apostolic decision, presided by James, not by Peter alone.
Paul withstanding Peter to his face, the Petrine office is not exempt from correction by a brother apostle.
